title: A closer look at loyalty of full-size pickup households
h1: A closer look at loyalty of full-size pickup households
metaDesc: Are full-size pickup owners truly the most loyal? New S&P Global Mobility data uncovers segment rankings, cross-pickup loyalty gains, and standout model loyalty trends.
summaryHtml:
Are full-size pickup owners truly the most loyal? New S&P Global Mobility data uncovers segment rankings, cross-pickup loyalty gains, and standout model loyalty trends.

  • Top 10 segments in loyalty, November 2025
  • Destination of full size half ton, three-quarter and one-ton pickup households
  • Brand loyalty by body style, household vs. disposal methodologies
  • Top 10 models in loyalty
  • Connect with our data experts for more industry insights

segments.html:
A generally accepted theory in the United States new vehicle industry is that full-size pickup households are among the most loyal, if not the most loyal, in the industry. S&P Global Mobility loyalty data, available at several levels, generally support this theory, but not always. 

A recent review of S&P Global Mobility segment loyalty data reveals that households with a full-size pickup in the garage are among the most loyal to the segment, but not the most loyal. Segment loyalty represents the percentage of return-to-market households in any given segment that acquire a new vehicle from the same segment (regardless of brand)
As shown in the following chart, the two full-size pickup segments rank #5 and #7 in loyalty among a total of 33 segments (only the top ten are displayed). Loyalty for the compact utility and three luxury utility segments all exceed segment loyalty for either full-size pickup segment.

A closer look at the data, however, reveals that when the two full-size pickup segments are combined, i.e., including migration from one to the other in either direction, loyalty to full-size pickups rises 8.2 percentage points for half-ton pickups and 11.2 percentage points for three-quarter/one-ton pickups (see the following two pie charts).  

When these incremental loyalty figures are added to the original segment results displayed in the previous chart, the results for both full-size segments surpass that of any other segment.

Destination of full-size three-quarter pickup households

segments.html:
These results are validated by body-style loyalty data, which represent the percent of return-to-market households with a model of a particular body style in the garage that acquire that same body style again. As illustrated below, pickup households—of which full-size pickup households make up about 75%—are the most loyal to the body style, and this is the case using either of the two S&P Global Mobility loyalty methodologies. 

The primary difference between the household and disposal loyalty methodologies is that, using the household methodology, the new vehicle acquired may or may not be a replacement for the original vehicle, while, using the disposal methodology, only those new vehicles that replace the original vehicle are included.

It is also noteworthy that the gap in body style loyalty between that obtained using the household methodology and that obtained using the disposal methodology is tied with the utility body style for greatest in the industry. This implies that the difference in body style loyalty between a household that may or may not replace the garage vehicle, and the household that definitely does replace its garage vehicle, is larger for pickup (and utility) households than for any other body style.  

Overall, return-to-market pickup households that are replacing their pickup are more loyal to the body style than those households that may or may not be replacing the original vehicle.  This intuitively makes sense, since a replacement vehicle is more likely to be similar to the original than a vehicle that may be an add to the fleet and therefore serving a different function.

Lastly, a review of model loyalty in November 2025 reinforces the strong model loyalty for full-size pickup households in general (see below). Of the 381 models with at least one retail registration in November, four of the six with the highest model loyalty (the percent of return-to-market households that acquire the same model) are full-size pickups.

Still looking at model loyalty, note that all four of the full-size pickups displayed on the chart above have model loyalty about twelve percentage points or more above the national average of 26.3%.

One last comment on the November model loyalty results: the Tesla Model Y occupies a unique position in the industry, as it is the only semi-mainstream utility (and that may be a stretch) offered by Tesla, limiting a Tesla loyalist to just that one model.  This suggests Model Y’s results may be positively impacted by the limited Tesla portfolio.  

The pickup represents a unique place in the US auto industry. Its market share does not equal that of utilities, but the pickup has been a core part of the industry since 1917, long before the first utility appeared, and the pickup stands at the heart of several mainstream brands to this day.  S&P Global Mobility data indicate pickup owners in general aren’t going anywhere.
